extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century London coffee-house readers; literate public and men of letters
extracted.subtask_description: Short, episodic literary and social commentary pieces (Tatler-style periodical essays) addressing manners, customs, law, literature, and current events for a coffee-house readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness in duels (customs to avoid advantage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dueling customs aimed to avoid any advantage between combatants: use of seconds to see that 'all was upon the square'; principals stripped to shirts to show they had nothing but what men of honour carry; weapons were to be equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: principals put on pumps and stripped to shirts; weapons of equal length were provided. This practice was intended to ensure an even contest and public accountability (the seconds were to make a faithful report). Anti-pattern: when seconds began to fight or when unequal weapons were used, fairness and the honour code were undermined (see Major Adroit story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and expected conduct of seconds
rubrics_metrics.description: Seconds were originally to stand by to ensure fairness and report the whole combat, but a fashion arose for seconds themselves to fight, and later social pressure made it shameful for a man of honour not to proffer himself as a second.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historic example: Major Adroit (second) was engaged by another second and fatally wounded, which led to seconds being expected to fight; later this produced over-participation (dozens per side). The text treats this as a dangerous fashion and explains how social incentives can pervert an originally procedural role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of weapons and procedures to prevent foul play
rubrics_metrics.description: Weapons should be equal (e.g., two swords of equal length) and procedures should minimize advantage (defensive fighting, equal arms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is perceived physical mismatch, parties switched to pistols. The narrative also notes rituals like stripping to shirts to prove nothing hidden. The account warns that customs intended to ensure equity can be subverted by fashion or cunning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pistols to neutralize physical advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: When an active, adroit, or strong man insulted an awkward or unpractised swordsman, combatants would resort to pistols to remove the advantage of swordsmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text discusses trade-offs: pistols can still favour a skilled marksman, and shaking hands or inexperience can disadvantage some—so even 'fair' methods may still produce morally fraught killings. The author notes a moral scruple about gaining honour by methods that make the result practically secure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yielding rule and its strategic effects
rubrics_metrics.description: A law among combatants held that the party whose first man was disarmed or killed should yield as vanquished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule affected incentives: it could encourage certain groups to quarrel (since only the 'very topping fellows' might be put at risk) and later made such fellows regard fighting as an incumbrance on their honour. The text uses this to explain the decline of certain fighting fashions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coin toss (cross or pile) to resolve who shoots
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid foul play and ensure fairness in pistol fights, parties could 'throw up cross or pile' (a coin toss) to decide who should be shot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as a pragmatic method that would remove opportunities for cheating and make outcomes less morally ambiguous when both must fight; recommended where honour requires a fair method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal standards for guardianship and estate protection for 'idiots' and 'fools'
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal practice: a lunatic (madman) is generally placed in the care of Chancery, while a 'fool' (idiot) is in the care of the Crown; the law vests possessions in the Crown to protect the estates of those lacking capacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and historical notes: inquiry into the capacity of a noble (Viscount Wenman) and discussion of the law's aim to protect family entails and industry of founders. The page debates the fairness of divesting estates from tractable or indolent persons versus crafty knaves who nevertheless display some reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between a fool and a madman (Lockean standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawing on Locke: a fool is one who from right principles makes a wrong conclusion; a madman is one who draws a just inference from false principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay uses the distinction to analyze behavior (the fool who commits a senseless act vs. the madman who acts consistently with his false belief). Both kinds of persons may be taken into custody, but the distinction helps explain differing outward conduct and perceived responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating an age's taste via stage characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The taste of an age is best discerned by observing the characters represented in its comedies; stage portrayals reflect social norms and what an era values or tolerates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ben Jonson's depiction of smoking as foppery; comparison of Shakespearean women's small part in dialogue reflecting their historical social freedom; modern stage women reflect increased freedom (virtuosas, coquettes). Use character types in drama as social evidence when judging a period's taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Playwrights should depict women as they are in their age
rubrics_metrics.description: A playwright's female characters should mirror the social reality of women in that era—their freedoms, conversational roles, and social functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Shakespeare drew women as they then were (mothers, sisters, wives) not from lack of genius; modern dramatists show women with more public wit and agency. This is offered as a criterion for evaluating the accuracy or social realism of dramatic portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style and rhetorical devices for lively battle narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain repetitive expressions and structural choices (e.g., 'Ditto,' 'And so,' 'But soon') and tactical subdivision of forces give life and spirit to relations of battles and exercises of arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay satirically praises a printed 'Exercise at Arms' for its vivid phrasing and novel method of subdividing and describing movements. Guidance: detailed, dynamic sequencing and emphatic small phrases can animate a narrative; choosing notable ground (e.g., Grub Street) gives historians eyewitness advantage. Also cautions that external contingencies (rain) can spoil intended effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of generous/loving passion (literary criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: True love is characterized as a tender, protecting affection that shows constant care for the beloved, abstracted from the lover's own interests—more generous than friendship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literary examples: Suckling's and Milton's pictured moments (lover watching sleeping beloved, Adam's 'cordial love'). The criterion is used to evaluate portrayals of love in literature: emphasis on guardianship, preservation, and self-abnegation rather than mere desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversation etiquette: diagnosis of the 'questioner' affectation
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'questioner' is someone who asks questions not to receive information but to affect an appearance of doubt and display modest ambition; such behaviour is a conversational vice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example behaviour: asking many leading or insincere questions at coffee-houses to show one's headiness rather than to learn (Will Why-not). The author recommends skepticism toward such performers and values straightforward inquiry over performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/patriotic criticism of affectation for foreign fashions
rubrics_metrics.description: The nation (England) is lamented for an affectation of everything foreign; this is presented as a negative standard—preference should be given to native events and achievements rather than idolizing foreign matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example complaint: a battle fought in London went unnoticed because attention was paid to foreign matters. The essay urges readers to value and attend to local events and native character rather than excessive admiration for foreign things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skeptical view of ostentatious claims to merit for public offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications for employment often rely on pity, spectacle, or trivial claims rather than genuine fitness for the place; merit should be the true criterion, not convenience or spectacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: tickets soliciting votes because a man had many children or because a dancing-master broke his leg; criticism of people seeking roles for convenience. The author implies employers/readers should judge candidates by competence, not affectation or dramatic appeals.
